text: you you you you Okay, I think it's been about 60. Hi, my name is Robin Martin. I'm Director of Media Services here at UC San Diego and I'm here to record a training sample of my voice and likeness for testing with AI generation tools. For this content, I want to talk a little bit about my job, how I got here from sort of outside industry, prior experience, a little bit of that just to give you a few minutes of sample to work from here. So my current job as Director of Media Services is actually over two teams here at the university. So there's the multimedia services team and the media teaching lab teams. I started here just over the multimedia services team in 2019. Actually, scratch that, 2018. Time flies when you're having fun and learning about all the goings-on here at the university. So I started in December of 2018. I had a couple of weeks of overlap with the outgoing retiring supervisor, so that was definitely a kind of heads down, drinking from the fire hose for a couple of weeks, learning all of those processes before they retired and left. This is also right before the holiday break, so had a couple weeks at the end of December and then leaving for a couple weeks and then coming back in January for a clean start in 2019. During that time, I was learning a lot about the current capabilities of the team, what the team's processes were for video production, for filming, what the studio facilities were like, what the editing processes were like, a couple of interesting projects that the team was already doing at that time. Studio U was in a kind of early beta phase and I was able to come in and help develop that to actually launch that with Jordy and Treb, who were on the team at that time. We also took the the spaces that I'm in recording in now and started to improve them. The team had started from a very small budget and had grown over time and so these rooms were very basic. They still had tile floors. Lights were just clamped onto the overhead structure of the room. We didn't have, you know, nice truss systems or sound absorption material on the walls, things like that, that would really help make the quality of the recordings in these spaces improve. So those were some of the early projects that we worked on in the space. And then the other main thing that we were working on 2019 was getting the Kaltura system up and running on campus. Kaltura is a video hosting platform and prior to that the team was really delivering a lot of content to either YouTube, which has some downsides because YouTube you can't necessarily control related videos or other content that comes up when you're on YouTube. Sometimes it's blocked for certain types of users. Not a great experience when you're trying to make sure students are just focusing on the educational content. Or the other process that the team was using at that time was publishing to Camtasia, which is a software that lets you wrap a video file in a flash player and play it through a web browser. I don't know if you remember what flash player was like, but those were kind of the dark days of the web in terms of interactivity and media capabilities required a lot of extra work, extra downloads for the folks in their browsers was not great. So Kaltura was going to be a big win for the university, let us kind of scale up a lot more of online education and video delivery for the campus. So that was another major effort back in 2019. In 2020, as we all know, the world changed out from under us in substantial ways and we had to learn how to do remote instruction on a massive scale all of a sudden. The university had a lot of capabilities in this area already. We were already using tools like Slack and Teams and Zoom in a limited fashion. We already had some people that were more or less fully remote or were working kind of on a hybrid basis. I got to do a trial run of this in 2019 when my wife broke her ankle and I had to all of a sudden take over care of my two sons for a little while. And so I was having to come to campus for a couple of hours in the middle of the day and then run home and get them from school and then continue trying to do meetings, email, things like that, remotely from home. So I had, I was prepared for it a little bit in 2020, but definitely it took a while to get the whole university and the team adapted to what remote work and hybrid work would look like as we kind of got through the pandemic phase. Also clearly it changed sort of our production processes and how we worked with faculty, how many people we could have in a room, masking mandates, people doing kind of wellness checks before they came to school to make sure they didn't have any symptoms, all those kinds of things. So all kinds of policy changes and process changes into 2021 as we kind of worked through those pandemic times. And then in 2022, we started to kind of resume more normal operations. The team was growing and we hired additional staff to help us provide more video production, additional producers were working on that. And then at the end of 2022, I took over the media teaching lab team when the manager who was over that team and had been for 15 or 20 years retired kind of all of a sudden out of the blue. So my boss Dan Suki asked me if I would be interested in helping cover that team too since they do analogous work. They're helping students develop and learn how to do media production. So learning, you know, the basics of a DSLR all the way up to, you know, Canon C100, Sony FS700s and higher-end types of film cameras and 16 millimeter film work as well, which I don't have a background in but the staff at the Media Lab do and I've actually really enjoyed learning a lot more about analog film production from them. So starting in 2022, I began helping the media teaching lab team as well. It was great for me to also see just a whole different side of the university after working here for a few years and see a lot more of the kind of in-person class delivery. The multimedia services team is so much about supporting remote and online instruction through video work and helping instructors record lectures and other kinds of content. But the media teaching lab is more about, okay, what is the very hands-on education that's happening on this campus? So it was nice for me to see more of that and get to learn more of the faculty, more of the departments that that group works with. Also the challenges of being in a building that's very old. That's one of the early buildings on campus. There's a studio space in that building that was, I think, put together back in the 60s or 70s. So it's been there for a very long time. Kind of the building is built around it. The rest of the departments are kind of around this very unique space. So learning how to take care of that space and learning how to kind of keep growing and evolving it so that it meets the needs of current productions. One of the studio spaces there still uses, you know, 2K tungsten lights, which is great, except for the fact that the electrical box that powers it is also about 60 years old and starting to fail. And so figuring out how we can work with facilities to keep that kind of very unique tool set and those facilities up and running while also in our more modern LED lighting-based space, continuing to evolve that and take advantage of newer fixtures and production processes in that space. One of the interesting projects that we have just done there is we took what used to be a full control room for live production TV studio class and shrunk that down into essentially a mobile cart. So going from a giant stream, I'm forgetting the name of the product, going from a giant essentially desk with monitors and switcher-based system to an ATM studio that fits on a cart with a couple of monitors and a couple of devices underneath it has been quite a shift because we needed that space for where that production room was for flats, storage for a prop room and things like that. So it's a fun kind of exercise in miniaturization and modernization and so far it's working pretty well and we've had a couple of classes use that system and it's great to see how the students pick that up, learn how to do a multi-camera live switched show both from the creative side and production design all the way through to the live capture. All right and then lastly outside of work I've had a kind of a varied athletic career. I started off playing you know soccer and little league when I was a kid. From there moved on to basketball and volleyball when I was in middle school and high school as I started to grow to to over six feet and especially growing up in Hawaii where there are not a lot of people over six feet I was definitely one of the taller ones and sports that took advantage of that were ideal. After high school when I went to college at SDSU I tried to get on to the volleyball team I came very close as a walk-on a couple of times and then played club and eventually was scouted by the rowing team. They had a pipeline of taking folks who didn't make it onto the some of the other teams that were still tall and athletic and getting them into rowing so I did that for a couple of years and competed for SDSU which was a ton of fun and then after school I got into mountain biking for a few years which was super fun. Some of my buddies in grad school were avid mountain bikers and they got me up to speed on mountain biking all around here in San Diego. There's tons of great trails and then since then I've really turned more towards trail running and ultra distances. The longest distance I've run so far is a 50k but I'm trying to work up towards a 50 miler maybe a hundred miler at some point down the road.
